parties:
Appellants: Paritosh Barua and Ors.
Vs.
Respondent: State and Ors.
full_judgment: "Even though section 80 of the Evidence Act provides for making certain presumption in respect of a confession by an accused person produced before a Court, taken in accordance with law and purporting to be signed by a Magistrate, we are of the view that having regard to the aforesaid facts noticed by the learned Judges it was at least injudicious to rely upon such confession without calling the Magistrate as a witness. The Court is required to see not only that the forms under sections 164 and 364 CrPC was complied with but the substance underneath the law was equally adhered to. There must not be any reason for doubt as to the truth of the statements, be it circumstantial or proved otherwise. In the circumstances of this particular case, it is difficult to deny the accused an opportunity to cross-examine the Magistrate who allegedly recorded their statements............In the instant case, admmitedly except the FIR and FIR cannot be used as substantive or primary evidence of the truth of its content. The First Information Report cannot be substituted for evidence given on oath, when there is no other evidence the facts mentioned in the information could not be relied upon as proof of the offence alleged. Therefore, the FIR which was proved in this case does not establish per se that there was an occurrence of dacoity as alleged. When there was thus no evidence of dacoity, of what use them it was to refer to the alleged confession of the accused to prove their purticipation in an occurrence which was not proved at all? It is true that in the confession itself there is a reference to the occurrence of dacoity and it may be said quite ingeniously that the confession itself proves the occurrence provided it is accepted. For the present purpose we think it sufficient to point out that the alleged confessions cannot be legally looked into, for, even the identity of the appellants as makers of the alleged confession has not been established by an evidence. Neither the police officer who took them to the Magistrate or forwarded them for recording confession nor the Magistrate himself was examined to prove that these were the persons who made the confessions which were recorded and produced before the court. Prosecution in the instant case completely failed for whatever reasons to bring on record the minimum legal evidence to prove that the occurrence of dacoity as alleged was committed and that the accused on the dock were the persons who made the confessions before a Magistrate (which were on record). We must therefore, hold that in the facts of the case there was no legal evidence before the court on basis of which the appellants could be lawfully convicted for the offense alleged, the learned Advocate appearing for the state has found it difficult to support the order of conviction."
